issues.legal_issue: Proceeds from selling trunks of trees of spontaneous growth are capital receipts rather than taxable income when the stumps and roots are left to protect land intended for cultivation, not to regenerate trees.
material_facts: The assessee sold trees of spontaneous growth that were interspersed among agricultural fields.
The agreement required the purchaser to leave the stumps and roots undisturbed and prohibited cutting the sprouts.
The assessee maintained that the restriction was intended to protect the soil so the cleared land could be used for cultivation, and the land was later partly converted to cultivable land.
The assessing authorities treated the proceeds as income, but the Tribunal did not reject the assessee’s account of the purpose of the restriction or find that the purpose was regeneration of trees.
issues.conclusion: The receipts were capital in nature and were not assessable to income tax. The Court upheld the High Court’s decision and dismissed the appeals, including the related appeals concerning assessment timing and penalties.
issues.legal_principle: The character of receipts from selling trees depends on the object and intention behind felling them. Under V. Venugopala Varma Rajah v. Commissioner of Income-tax, Kerala, 76 ITR 460, receipts from trunks may be income where the stumps remain capable of regeneration and the trees are felled with an object of producing further returns. A sale that removes the roots and ends the source may be capital under A. K. T. K. M. Vishnudatta Antharjanam v. Commissioner of Agricultural Income Tax, Trivandrum, 78 ITR 58, which applied the test in Commissioner of Income Tax, Bengal v. Shaw, Wallace and Co., 6 I.T.C. 178. But leaving stumps and roots intact does not by itself establish a profit-making activity: where the evidence shows that they were left to protect land intended for cultivation and regeneration was not intended, the proceeds are capital. The department had to reject the assessee’s account and establish that regeneration was the object before treating the receipts as revenue. The related assessment and penalty appeals were dismissed as consequences of the ruling on the principal issue.

rule.if: income_tax_assessment_of_tree_sale_receipts and trees_of_spontaneous_growth_sold and stumps_and_roots_left_intact and restriction_intended_to_protect_land_for_cultivation and not owner_intended_tree_regeneration and land_later_put_to_cultivation and department_did_not_reject_cultivation_purpose

predicates.income_tax_assessment_of_tree_sale_recei: The proceeding concerns whether receipts from selling trees are taxable income.
predicates.trees_of_spontaneous_growth_sold: The owner sold trees that had grown spontaneously.
predicates.stumps_and_roots_left_intact: The purchaser was required to leave the stumps and roots in the ground.
predicates.restriction_intended_to_protect_land_for: The restriction on removing stumps and roots was intended to protect the land for cultivation.
predicates.owner_intended_tree_regeneration: The owner intended the trees to regenerate so that they could produce further returns.
predicates.land_later_put_to_cultivation: The owner later put at least part of the cleared land to cultivation.
predicates.department_did_not_reject_cultivation_pu: The tax authority did not reject the owner’s account that the restriction protected land intended for cultivation.

issues.definition: When an income-tax assessment concerns the sale of spontaneously grown trees, the stumps and roots remain, the restriction protects land for cultivation, regeneration was not intended, cultivation later occurs, and the tax authority does not reject that purpose, the receipts are treated as capital rather than taxable income.
